paragraphs.text: Childhood cancer is the second leading cause of death in children aged 1–14 years, exceeded in the United States only by accidents [1]. About 400,000 children aged 0–19 years are estimated to develop cancer every year, approximately 90% in low- and middle-income countries [2]. Advances in the treatment of pediatric cancers have resulted in increasing numbers of children surviving their malig nancy, with current survival rates greater than 85% in 5 years in high-income countries [1].
paragraphs.heading: 38.1 Introduction

paragraphs.text: The most common childhood malignan cies are leukemias (28.8%), followed by cen tral nervous system (CNS) tumors (24.0%) and lymphomas (11.2%) [3]. Acute lympho blastic leukemia (ALL) accounts for about 80% of childhood leukemia cases [4]. Brain tumors are the largest group of solid tumors in children and adolescents, with medullo blastoma being the most frequent malignant neoplasm of the CNS [5]. Craniopharyngioma corresponds to 5–10% of pediatric CNS tumors [5].
Therapeutic options consist of multiagent chemotherapy, surgery, radiotherapy, and bone marrow or stem cell transplantation. As

expected, decreased mortality from malig nancy comes at the cost of increased morbid ity resulting from acute and late effects of different treatment modalities. Endocrine dis orders affect up to 60% of childhood cancer survivors (CCS) and may occur soon after treatment or many years after cure of malig nancy [6]. Obesity, malnutrition, metabolic syndrome, secondary malignancies, and growth disturbances are frequent conse quences of cancer treatment during childhood [6]. Up to 49% of children who have under gone cranial irradiation developed at least one hormone deficiency. Growth hormone defi ciency (GHD) is the most frequent, followed by either thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) or gonadotropin deficiency. Adrenocortico tropic hormone (ACTH) deficiency is the least common and permanent diabetes insipidus (DI) is very rare [6–9]. Risk factors for endo crine deficiencies include total radiation dose, age at treatment, and time since last treatment [7]. More recently, immune checkpoint inhibi tors, such as ipilimumab, have been found to be associated with hypophysitis with or with out hypopituitarism, thyroid dysfunction, and, in rare cases, adrenalitis [10]. Therefore, lifelong follow-up of CCS, including screen ing for endocrine dysfunction, is recom mended to ensure early diagnosis and appropriate treatment. This chapter will describe the more frequently acute and late endocrine effects of cancer treatment during childhood.

Children with tumors that involve the hypothalamic-pituitary (HP) region, such as craniopharyngiomas or germinomas, may present hypothalamic-pituitary axis (HPA) dysfunction before tumor treatment or soon after the therapeutic procedure. Growth fail ure, obesity, delayed puberty, and central DI related to compression and/or invasion of the HP axis are frequently seen. Deficiencies in GH, gonadotropins, and ACTH are reported in 75%, 60%, and 30% of patients, respectively [11, 12]. Whenever possible, a complete endo
paragraphs.heading: of Brain Tumors Treatment

paragraphs.text: crinologic evaluation should be performed before initiating treatment [12].
paragraphs.heading: of Brain Tumors Treatment

paragraphs.text: Most cases of central DI are secondary to destruction or degeneration of the neurons originating in the supraoptic and paraventric ular nuclei and may be a presenting symptom of Langerhans cell histiocytosis, germinoma and craniopharyngioma. A destruction of 80–90% of the hypothalamic vasopressin (AVP) or antidiuretic hormone (ADH) neu rons is required to produce DI. As a result, even large lesions in the sellar and suprasellar area generally are not associated with impaired water homeostasis until they are sur gically resected. Intraoperative damage of AVP neurons during HP surgery is one of the most common causes of central DI, corre sponding to 20% of all cases [13].
paragraphs.heading: of Brain Tumors Treatment

paragraphs.text: Sodium alterations are common after transsphenoidal surgery (TSS) of the pitu itary gland, but they are generally transitory with normal AVP secretion and diuresis at 7–14 postoperative days [13]. Triphasic response that consists of initial central DI (1–4 days) followed by syndrome of inappro priate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) (4–7 days) due to the release of AVP from degenerating neurons, and finally, per manent DI is often noted after prolonged neurosurgery [14, 15]. Symptoms of DI are consisting of high-volume output of dilute urine, hypovolemia, and hypernatremia. Local edema at the surgical site and interruption of normal AVP secretion are thought to be caus ative. The duration of this first phase is vari able, so intravenous AVP infusion might be needed. Coexisting hypothyroidism and adre nal insufficiency may mask the symptoms of DI due to reduced free water clearance [16, 17]. Transient SIADH usually occurs 4–7 days postoperative and is associated with postop erative morbidity. It develops from the uncon trolled release of AVP by degenerating pituitary nerve terminals containing neurose cretory granules [15]. This unregulated release of AVP results in inappropriately decreased urinary output with high urinary osmolality (>200 mOsm/kg), hypervolemia, and mod estly elevated urinary sodium concentrations (>20–30 mEq/L). Fluid restriction is recom mended for treatment [18–20]. Finally, if more
paragraphs.heading: of Brain Tumors Treatment

paragraphs.text: than 90% of AVP neurons are damaged, patients develop the third phase of permanent DI. At this point, the treatment of choice for central DI is intranasal or oral desamino-darginine vasopressin (DDAVP).
paragraphs.heading: of Brain Tumors Treatment

paragraphs.text: Another hyponatremic condition virtu ally indistinguishable from SIADH is cere bral salt wasting (CSW), a less common condition primarily seen, but not exclusively, in neurosurgical patients associated with CNS disease. In CSW, there is inappropriate and excessive release of natriuretic peptides leading to a primary natriuresis and volume depletion. The mechanism behind the devel opment of CSW probable involves disrup tion of neural input to the kidneys along with the stimulated release of natriuretic fac tors. The main difference is the absence or presence of volume depletion: CSW presents with hyponatremia, clinical evidence of dehydration (not always present), inappro priately concentrated urine, and renal sodium wasting, often in the setting of acute head injury, bleed, or surgery. It may be differenti ated from SIADH based on the persistence of hypouricemia and increased fractional excretion of urate following the correction of hyponatremia. The preferred therapy for the treatment of hyponatremia in patients with CSW is 3% sodium chloride [19, 20].
paragraphs.heading: of Brain Tumors Treatment

paragraphs.text: During treatment for pediatric cancer, mal nutrition, and cachexia are common situa tions. Chemotherapy, radiation, surgery, and immunotherapy directly result in nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, malabsorption, stomati tis, esophagitis, and anorexia. Malnutrition can compromise immunity leading to higher infection rates, neuropathy, worse physical function and quality of life [21]. Tumorinduced cytokine production initiates a cas cade of metabolic events including glycogenolysis, lipolysis, proteolysis, increased resting energy expenditure, and
paragraphs.heading: Weight Gain, and Hyperglycemia During Cancer Treatment

paragraphs.text: gluconeogenesis [22]. It should be noted that pediatric patients with ALL can experience significant weight gain at the beginning of treatment secondary to reduced physical activity and to high-dose glucocorticoid treatment [23]. Hyperglycemia, insulin resis tance, dyslipidemia, central adiposity, and hepatic steatosis may also be precipitated by glucocorticoids [24]. l-asparaginase, which is often combined with glucocorticoids in the treatment of ALL, has toxic effects on the beta-cell and has been associated with the development of transient or persistent diabe tes mellitus [25].
paragraphs.heading: Weight Gain, and Hyperglycemia During Cancer Treatment

paragraphs.text: Many factors may cause poor growth in CCS including poor nutrition and low body mass index (BMI), long-term treatment with gluco corticoids, GHD, CPP, hypothyroidism, and spi nal irradiation [27, 28]. GHD may occur as the result of direct tumor invasion, surgery, and cra nial irradiation [31]. The average time between completion of tumor treatment and the onset of poor longitudinal growth has been reported as 37.7 months in children treated with radiother apy [32], ranging from 3 months to 5 years [33]. The risk of short adult height is higher when radiotherapy is given at younger age and before puberty, with higher risk in those treated between 6 and 10 years of age [26, 34, 35]. The hypothala mus might be affected with lower doses of irra
paragraphs.heading: Hormone Deficiency

paragraphs.text: diation compared with the pituitary [36, 37], and the somatotrophs are the more vulnerable pitu itary cells to radiotherapy [38–40]. GHD has been associated with radiotherapy doses ≥18 Gy to the HP region as well as with total body irra diation (TBI) using a 10 Gy single dose or frac tionated doses totaling 12 Gy [26]. GHD may appear after 12 months if the dose is greater than 60 Gy, in 36 months if the dose is between 25 and 30 Gy, and in 60 months if the dose is between 15 to 20 Gy [41]. The pituitary height might be significantly reduced after radiother apy, possibly due to radiation-induced pituitary cell apoptosis, or because radiation may affect vascular function and oxygen supply [42]. Antipituitary and antihypothalamus autoanti bodies were demonstrated in 47.8% of children irradiated due to craniopharyngioma, germi noma, or gliomas, compared with none in 50 healthy controls [43]. This implies that RT may have an indirect effect by triggering an inappro priate immune attack on the pituitary tissues by autoantibodies [7]. Spinal irradiation is an inde pendent risk factor for growth impairment and may result in disproportionate growth more evi dent during puberty [44].
paragraphs.heading: Hormone Deficiency

paragraphs.text: GHD is unlikely after traditional chemo therapy, but some newer agents may interfere with normal growth by affecting growth plates or dysregulating growth hormone-insulin-like growth factor-I (GH-IGF-I) signaling path ways (tyrosine kinase inhibitors, TKI) or caus ing an autoimmune hypophysitis (immune checkpoint inhibitors) [34, 45]. Some alkylat ing agents, such as busulfan and lomustine, are independent risk factor for short stature, par ticularly after leukemia or neuroblastoma, and are also risk factors for gonadal dysfunction, which may further exacerbate growth impair ment [30]. Other chemotherapy agents may directly damage the growth plates and cause severe short stature, such as cis-retinoic acid for the treatment of neuroblastoma and hedge hog pathway inhibitors [46, 47].
paragraphs.heading: Hormone Deficiency

paragraphs.text: Growth of children who have undergone can cer treatment should be assessed every 6–12 months, and lifelong assessment may be necessary to screen for the development of
paragraphs.heading: Cancer Treatment

paragraphs.text: GHD. It is recommended to measure standing and sitting height in children treated with spi nal radiotherapy, craniospinal irradiation, as well as radiation to the chest, abdomen, or pelvis [26, 48]. Establishing the diagnosis of GHD can be challenging and should be made in the context of clinical findings, as a growth deceleration of at least 0.3 SDS/year or height deviation from the familial background [49], and laboratory evaluation. It is important to avoid false-positive tests in the diagnosis of GHD, with special attention to obesity, a common condition in some CCS [50]. The Pediatric Endocrine Society guidelines suggest that the diagnosis of GHD without using a GH dynamic test can be made in patients with the following conditions: auxological criteria as mentioned before, HP defect (such as major congenital malformation, tumor, or irradia tion), and deficiency of at least one additional pituitary hormone [51]. In patients with a high probability of GHD (poor growth, other pitu itary hormones deficiencies), one GH provoc ative test is sufficient to make the diagnosis, after excluding other growth failure etiologies (e.g., total body irradiation, imatinib mesyl ate, and cis-retinoic acid treatment) [50]. The insulin tolerance test has been considered the gold standard provocative stimulation test to make the diagnosis of GHD, but caution should be exerted and alternative secreta gogues (i.e., glucagon) should be considered in patients at risk for seizures [50, 52, 53]. Growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) alone or in combination with arginine is not recom mended in CCS after HP irradiation because radiation doses less than 40 Gy cause predom inantly hypothalamic damage, and conse quently, exogenous hypothalamic hormones administration may cause false-negative results [26, 28]. Radiation-induced reduction of somatostatin secretion result in greater tonic GH release from the remaining somato trophs [37], and the decreased GH pulse amplitude has been shown to be secondary to decreased GHRH secretion [37]. GH neurose cretory dysfunction has been associated with low-dose radiation exposure, with a preserved peak GH response on dynamic tests, despite decreased endogenous GH secretion [54]. During puberty, these patients do not present
paragraphs.heading: Cancer Treatment

paragraphs.text: an appropriate acceleration in growth velocity due to a lack of increased GH secretion [54, 55]. The measurement of serum IGF-I levels is not recommended as a biomarker for the diag nosis of GHD in CCS, especially among those exposed to HP irradiation [26]. Normal serum IGF-I and insulin-like growth factor binding protein-3 (IGFBP-3) levels have been observed in CCS who failed in GH dynamic testing, with abnormal growth velocity and GHD, especially those treated with low doses of radiotherapy [56, 57]. The use of IGF-I as a screening tool should be restricted to patients treated with high cranial radiation doses [58].
paragraphs.heading: Cancer Treatment

paragraphs.text: Treatment with GH is usually indicated in CCS with proven GHD after careful discus sion with the patient, his/her family if appro priate, as well as with the treating oncologist or neurosurgeon. The most appropriate and safest time to start GH is still a topic of debate, primarily due to a paucity of data and lack of controlled trials [59]. The timing of initiation of GH therapy following comple tion of cancer therapy or treatment of an intracranial tumor depends on many factors and should be individualized, with reports of treatment starting as early as 3 months in chil dren with radiologically proven stable cranio pharyngiomas who have significant growth and metabolic disturbances [52]. The Endocrine Society and the Pediatric Endocrine Society guidelines suggest waiting for 12 months after completing cancer treatments [26, 51]. In children with residual tumor and stable disease, as is often the case with optic pathway tumors and low-grade gliomas, the safety and timing of the initiation of GH treatment should specifically be discussed with the oncologist [26]. GH doses are similar to those used for the treatment of GHD in non-CCS [26, 51], with a starting dose of 0.022–0.035 mg/kg/day and individualization of subsequent dosing [51]. Long-acting GH preparations have different pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics than daily GH [60, 61], and current safety data in CCS are very limited [52]. The safety of GH replacement for children on treatment with TKI has not
paragraphs.heading: Cancer Treatment

paragraphs.text: been established and therefore is not recom mended at the present time [26, 52].

GH replacement therapy has been shown to increase growth velocity and adult height in CCS with GHD [29, 63]. However, cranio spinal irradiation or TBI might interfere with the response to treatment. The greatest determinants of adult height are height at the beginning of GH replacement and the interval between the end of cancer treatment and the beginning of GH [64]. In children who received spinal irradiation, GH may result in improvement in lower limb length, but not in spine and total height, increasing body disproportion that becomes most apparent during the time of the pubertal growth spurt [26, 65].

The treatment with GH in CCS carries additional safety concerns. Scoliosis is com mon following either spinal surgery and/or spinal or craniospinal irradiation [26, 66], and GH therapy may exacerbate this condi tion due to rapid growth [51]. Slipped capi tal femoral epiphysis is more frequently seen during GH treatment in GHD follow ing intracranial neoplasms, craniopharyn gioma and after bone marrow transplantation, compared with patients with idiopathic GHD. GH replacement is also associated with a slightly increased risk of intracranial hypertension [51].
paragraphs.heading: After Cancer Treatment

paragraphs.text: The risk of developing tumor recurrence and/or a second neoplasm is an important consideration during follow-up of cancer
paragraphs.heading: After Cancer Treatment

paragraphs.text: survivors. The most frequently reported sec ond neoplasms are non-melanoma skin can cer, breast cancer, meningiomas, thyroid cancer, soft tissue sarcomas, and CNS tumors, by the order of frequency [67, 68]. Genetic factors and adverse effects from cancer treat ment may synergize in raising the risk among survivors [40]. Cranial radiotherapy is known to increase the risk for developing meningi oma [68, 69]. While a nonsignificant associa tion was reported between GH replacement therapy and recurrence of the primary cancer, studies have reported that treatment with GH may increase the risk for a secondary tumor in CCS [70–76]. In the SAGhE cohort, from 10,403 patients treated with GH, 38 were diagnosed with meningioma. Thirty of them had been treated with craniospinal radiother apy, given a standardized incidence ratio
paragraphs.heading: After Cancer Treatment

paragraphs.text: (SIR) for meningioma in the overall cohort of 75.4 [77]. However, the risk of meningioma was not increased in patients whose diagnosis before GH treatment was not cancer (SIR = 2.4). No significant associations were observed between the risk for meningioma and age of start GH treatment, time since starting treatment, mean daily GH dose, dura tion of treatment, or cumulative dose of GH [77]. Sklar et al. [71] reported an increased risk of second solid neoplasms with GH (RR, 3.21) in survivors of acute leukemia/lym phoma (RR, 4.98), with no secondary leuke mias. In a control-matched study with patients treated with CNS irradiation followed up to 14.5 years, the recurrency\e or incidence of secondary tumors did not differ significantly between GH-treated patients and controls [62]. The risk of GH-dependent effects on sec
paragraphs.heading: After Cancer Treatment

paragraphs.text: ondary tumor was 10% in both GH-treated and untreated patients with a mean latency time of 22.5 years [62], and meningiomas were the most frequent second tumor in the GHtreated groups [62, 78, 79]. Female sex, young age at primary cancer diagnosis, a long period since cranial irradiation [80], CNS radiation dose ≥20 Gy, and cumulative doses of multi ple alkylating agents were associated with meningioma development [81]. These reports reinforce the need to interpret cautiously the risk of secondary tumors in GH treated patients. It is advisable to consider the rela tively small number of events, high confidence intervals, and low levels of significance. In addition, there is the risk of outcome bias as CCS are already at increased risk of second neoplasm [77]. A recent consensus stated that the effect of GH replacement on the risk of secondary neoplasia is minor compared with host and tumor treatment-related factors. The current evidence does not support an associa tion between treatment with GH and primary tumour or cancer recurrence and increase mortality from cancer among CCS with treated GHD [52].
paragraphs.heading: After Cancer Treatment

paragraphs.text: Thyroid hormone dysfunction is common in CCS, with increased risk for primary hyper thyroidism, and both primary and central hypothyroidism. Primary hypothyroidism is reported in 4%, 7%, and 13% after a mean thyroid irradiation dose of 10, 20, and 30 Gy, respectively [82]. Subclinical hypothyroidism is more common and may be transient. The younger the age, the higher the risk, with the greatest risk before 5 years of age. While most patients (65%) will develop primary hypothy roidism 5 years or more after radiation [83, 84], the risk of developing radiation-related hypothyroidism remains elevated even >25 years after exposure [84]. Benign nodules and thyroid malignancies can also occur after head and neck irradiation or TBI before BMT [85–88]. Given the impact of thyroid status on growth and development, appropriate lifelong monitoring is necessary to recognize these dis
paragraphs.heading: Abnormalities

paragraphs.text: orders and initiate appropriate treatment [87]. Annual thyroid and cervical lymph node eval uation on physical examination and annual free thyroxine and TSH measurements are necessary after external radiation or 131I-metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG), and before and periodically during immunother apy or TKI therapy (sunitinib). In thyrotoxic patients, thyrotropin receptor antibody (TRAb) should be measured to assess for autoimmune thyroid disease. Ultrasonogra phy and fine needle aspiration biopsy are indi cated if a palpable abnormality is identified [87]. However, small or posterior nodules may not be appreciated by palpation. Although there are no formal guidelines regarding the use of thyroid ultrasonography for regular screening for secondary thyroid malignancies, it is suggested to start the assessment 5 years after radiotherapy or MIBG treatment and it might be repeated every 3–5 years [48, 89, 90].

Children treated for Hodgkin disease have a relative risk for hypothyroidism of 17.1 times compared with sibling controls; in patients treated with 45 Gy or more, the risk of hypo thyroidism is 50% at 20 years from diagnosis [82]. Other agents known to cause primary hypothyroidism are MIBG, 131-iodine, TKI, immune checkpoint inhibitors, interferon-α, and interleukin-2 [45, 87]. After the last drug exposure, hypothyroidism may be preceded by a thyrotoxic phase due to destructive thyroid itis [87]. To mitigate the risks to the thyroid gland during MIBG therapy, potassium iodide alone or in combination with potassium per chlorate or methimazole and exogenous thy roxine have been used to block thyroidal uptake, with conflicting results [87].

Central hypothyroidism, or TSH defi ciency, occurs after injury of the HP axis due to tumor growth, surgery, and/or radiother apy. TSH deficiency is more likely to occur with exposure to higher cranial radiation doses (≥30 Gy) [8, 91]. Medications such as bexarotene (a synthetic retinoid X receptorselective), immune checkpoint inhibitors and mitotane may also cause TSH deficiency [87]. In CCS with central hypothyroidism, declin ing free thyroxine levels have been associated with weight gain, dyslipidemia, and glucose disorders [87, 92].

Thyroid hormone replacement in CCS is safe, even though thyroid hormones are known to play a role in oncogenic pathways involving cell growth, apoptosis inhibition, and stimula tion of angiogenesis [92]. l-thyroxine replace ment should only be started after evaluating other hormonal deficiencies, especially adrenal insufficiency, as thyroid hormone can acceler ate cortisol clearance and can precipitate an acute adrenal crisis [93]. Primary hyperthyroid ism after external radiation is uncommon. It is known that thyroid radiation may cause tran sient thyrotoxicosis, followed by euthyroidism or hypothyroidism. The highest risk is in patients receiving >30 Gy [87].

Irradiation of the thyroid gland is a signifi cant risk factor for the development of both benign and malignant thyroid neoplasms. The cumulative incidence of thyroid neoplasia con tinues to rise even 30 years after the primary cancer diagnosis [87], and it accounts for about 10% of subsequent malignancies in CCS, spe cifically papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) [87, 94]. Survivors of childhood Hodgkin disease are 18.3-fold more likely to develop PTC. The greatest risk for the development of thyroid can cer appears to involve children treated before 10 years of age and/or with doses in the range of 20–39.9 Gy [94]. Therefore, the risk of thyroid neoplasia is elevated at any radiation dose. This likely reflects the direct cytotoxic effect of irra diation, which results in fewer thyrocytes that could eventually undergo malignant transfor mation [87]. The MIBG therapy is also associ ated with the increased risk of thyroid neoplasms [87]. Radiation-induced thyroid cancers are not more aggressive than sporadic disease. However, PTC after radiation may be associated with multifocality and cervical lymph node metasta ses [87]. An additional increased cancer risk has been reported among recipients of alkylating chemotherapy. However, not all studies have found a strong risk of thyroid cancer following exposure to chemotherapy [87, 94].
The gonadal axis abnormalities in CCS include central precocious puberty, delayed puberty, and hypogonadism.
paragraphs.heading: 38.4.3 Gonadal Axis Abnormalities

paragraphs.text: Precocious puberty is defined as the onset of thelarche before the age of 8 years in girls, and testicular enlargement before the age of 9 years in boys. Children with CNS tumors near the hypothalamus or optic pathways are at increased risk of CPP [8]. CPP or puberty acceleration can also occur after cranial radio therapy (18–50 Gy) to any area of the CNS, not necessarily the HP region, and CPP is consid ered by some authors to be the second most common endocrine dysfunction after radio therapy [95]. Risk factors are young age, female sex, and increased BMI. Girls are more affected than boys following lower-dose irradiation (16–24 Gy), while higher radiation doses (25–50 Gy) lead to CPP in both sexes equally [96, 97]. The mechanism for CPP following irra diation is hypothesized to involve the dysregula tion of cortical influences on the hypothalamus and the release of the inhibitory GABAnergic tone [96, 98, 99]. Testicular volume may be a less reliable indicator of pubertal onset in boys who have received gonadotoxic chemotherapy and/or testicular radiation. Damage to the sem iniferous tubules during treatment may result in atrophic testes that are incapable of enlarging during pubertal progression. Therefore, the assessment of other secondary sexual charac teristics on physical examination is necessary [100]. The increase in growth velocity due to puberty can delay the diagnosis of GHD, or a blunted or absent growth spurt due to concom itant GHD may occur. Treatment with a depot gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) analogue may be indicated [95].
paragraphs.heading: 38.4.3.1 Central Precocious Puberty

paragraphs.text: Delayed puberty and hypogonadism are fre quent complications in CCS. Delayed puberty can result from primary gonadal injury (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism) or defi ciency of central activating signals (hypogo nadotropic hypogonadism) [34, 101]. CCS patients at risk of hypogonadism must be asked about onset and tempo of puberty, and menstrual history, and Tanner staging should be performed annually until sexual maturity [34]. High-dose cranial irradiation (>40 Gy) affects the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal
paragraphs.heading: Hypogonadism, and Fertility

paragraphs.text: (HPG) axis and is associated with hypogo nadotropic hypogonadism within the context of combined hormonal pituitary deficiencies [7, 101]. CCS with a history of exposure to radiotherapy, including abdominal/pelvic, TBI, and craniospinal radiation, and/or alkyl ating agents are at increased risk of gonadal failure. Additionally, gonadal failure had been described in patients after treatment with 131-radioiodine for differentiated thyroid car cinoma, and after MIBG for neuroblastoma treatment [34].
paragraphs.heading: Hypogonadism, and Fertility

paragraphs.text: The main chemotherapeutic agents with a gonadotoxic effect are the alkylating agents, alone or in combination. It is difficult to establish the isolated effect of each medica tion, as protocols generally use them in com bination, so the dose equivalent to cyclophosphamide (CED) must be calculated. The use of CED >6000 mg/m2 is a high-risk factor for gonadal failure. TKIs, in addition to causing central hypogonadism due to hypophysitis, can induce an inflammatory response in the gonads, leading to gonadal dysfunction and infertility [34, 101–103]. Radiotherapy worsens the gonadotoxic effect of alkylating agents [34, 101]. BMT can affect the gonads during conditioning, with the use of gonadotoxic drugs, associated with or without whole-body radiation and high-dose glucocorticoids. About 83% of patients will have hypogonadism after BMT [8, 9, 88].
paragraphs.heading: Hypogonadism, and Fertility

paragraphs.text: Diagnosis of hypogonadism is based on laboratory testing, which includes morning LH, FSH, and total testosterone (boys) or estradiol (girls) levels, and bone age radiogra phy to assess skeletal maturity until epiphy seal fusion [8, 48, 88, 103]. As primary and central hypogonadism can coexist in CCS with multiple therapies, LH and FSH will have little diagnostic value in these patients [8]. Treatment should be initiated at adequate age for both sexes [48, 88, 103]. Surgical, med ical, and technological advances have enabled the medical community to provide fertility options for patients with cancer and cancer survivors. Discussion of the impact of cancer treatment on fertility and a review of options of fertility preservation are recommended during cancer diagnosis and treatment with patients and their families [104–113].
paragraphs.heading: Hypogonadism, and Fertility

paragraphs.text: Hypogonadism may be suspected in CCS girls with no signs of puberty at 13 years-old, failure in pubertal progression, menstrual irregularity, primary amenorrhea at 16 years, or secondary amenorrhea [34, 48, 88]. Chemotherapy drugs, particularly alkylating drugs such as busulfan, cyclophosphamide, lomustine, and procarba zine, are harmful to the ovaries by causing damage to the DNA of the growing follicles and germ cells depletion. Older age and more advanced pubertal stage are susceptible to lower doses with reduction of ovarian follicles and premature ovarian insufficiency (POI). POI is a clinical condition characterized by the absence of menstrual cycles for 4 or more months and two elevated serum FSH levels in the menopausal range at an age younger than 40 years [103]. Ovarian damage occurs due to direct exposition to radiation during pelvic or low abdominal, lumbosacral, spinal, and TBI, and depends on the dose, number of fractions, and age of exposure to radiotherapy. Ovaries of younger girls are more resistant to damage from irradiation [114, 115]. Increasing ovarian irradiation dose and exposure to procarbazine and cyclophosphamide at ages 13–20 years are independent risk factors for the development of acute ovarian failure [114] .
paragraphs.heading: and Fertility

paragraphs.text: Decreased ovarian reserve can be demon strated by low anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) levels, low ovarian surface area, and high FSH levels [103, 114]. AMH is produced by the granulosa cells of preantral and small antral follicles and is present at low levels in prepubertal females and increases to a peak around age 25 years. It decreases with age, and with the decreasing reserve of ovarian folli cles. It is not recommended as a screening for POI, but it might be used to assess female fer tility at greater than 25 years [88, 103, 114]. Radiation affects not only the ovary but also the uterus and can cause vascular injury, endothelial damage and fibrosis in the myo metrium, increasing the risk of miscarriage, preterm delivery, small for gestational age birth, and postpartum hemorrhage, with impact on younger women [114]. Some stud ies have shown that ovarian dysfunction can be transient and may not require hormone
paragraphs.heading: and Fertility

paragraphs.text: replacement [116]. Spontaneous recovery of gonadal function after TKI may occur [102]. Some patients will have permanent POI with infertility and estrogen deficiency, but others will show recovery allowing fertility, although their reproductive life may be shorter [88, 103]. Alkylating agents and radiation dose of >30 Gy or ovarian/uterine radiation doses ≥5 Gy are associated with a decreased proba bility of spontaneous pregnancy [117].
paragraphs.heading: and Fertility

paragraphs.text: Treatment for female hypogonadism aims to induce and maintain secondary sexual char acteristics, to promote growth without acceler ating fusion of the growth plates, normalize uterine growth, avoid sexual dysfunction, and promote proper acquisition of bone mass. Induction of thelarche is achieved by using estrogen with gradual dose escalation starting at 11–12 years of age until menarche is achieved. After menarche (or after 2 years of starting estrogen replacement if no spontane ous bleeding occurs), progesterone must be added to promote cycling, in the same scheme as for other causes of hypogonadism. However, 17-β-estradiol is the treatment of choice [118]. However, for convenience, a combination estrogen-progestin oral contraceptive pill can be introduced after the patient is on full replace ment doses of estrogen. Delaying the onset of puberty in girls who were diagnosed late and have short stature should be discussed with the girl and her family. Hypopituitary women treated with GH should receive estrogen replacement preferably by a nonoral route, as oral estrogen reduces serum IGF-I response to GH therapy [119]. To reduce the cytotoxic effects of radiation and chemotherapy, some investigators have tried maintaining germinal epithelium quiescence by creating an artificial prepubescent state using a GnRH agonist [106, 108, 120]. However, there are no current con sensus guidelines on the use of GnRH agonists to preserve fertility during chemotherapy and/ or radiotherapy [34, 106].

paragraphs.text: Hypoandrogenism may manifest clinically as delayed or arrested puberty: no signs of puberty after 14 years of age, or absence of pubertal progress over 6–8 months. Annual
paragraphs.heading: and Fertility

paragraphs.text: assessment of pubertal development is recom mended until sexual maturity for CCS treated with gonadotoxic therapy before the onset of puberty. Testicular volume may not increase as expected during puberty in patients who received gonadotoxic therapy [34, 48, 121, 122]. Young men treated with gonadotoxic therapies after puberty should be assessed annually for symptoms of hypoandrogenism (decreased libido, decreased spontaneous erections, gynecomastia, loss of body hair, decreased muscle bulk or testicular volume, and hot flashes) [123]. A possible association between gynecomastia and TKI use has been reported [45].
paragraphs.heading: and Fertility

paragraphs.text: Testicular radiation, gonadotoxic chemo therapy, orchiectomy, cranial surgery, or cen tral radiation involving the HP axis can result in primary or secondary hypogonadism. Testicular tissue is more sensitive to radiation than ovarian tissue, and Sertoli cells are com paratively more sensitive than Leydig cells. In adults, testicular damage has been described at doses between 0.2–0.7 Gy, with an increase in FSH levels and changes in semen analysis. Exposure to conditioning doses of 10–12 Gy during TBI before puberty may lead to small testicular volume in the adult with damage of the seminiferous tubules and spermatogonia [121, 123]. Low doses of radiation, such as the 2 Gy used in TBI, and low doses of chemo therapy can deplete the spermatogonia pool through direct DNA damage resulting in per manent infertility [121, 123]. Azoospermia is described with doses of 6–10 Gy and Leydig cell failure with doses ≥20 Gy. In the series of CCS treated with chemotherapy and radio therapy at doses of 30–45 Gy, it was reported that 83% suffered from azoospermia. However, 17% recovered spermatogenesis 12–15 years after treatment [101, 121–123]. Inhibin B secreted by Sertoli cells can be use ful for screening for gonadal damage. In pre pubescent children, together with FSH, it can be used to assess gonadotoxic potential [101, 103, 122].
paragraphs.heading: and Fertility

paragraphs.text: Testosterone replacement is the primary treatment for male hypogonadism. The goals of therapy are similar to girls to induce normal pubertal development, maintain secondary sexual characters, avoid sexual dysfunction,
paragraphs.heading: and Fertility

paragraphs.text: improve bone density, and increase lean mass. Testosterone replacement may be initiated at 14 years of age at low doses (50 mg/month) and increased every 6 months to reach full adult replacement (200–250 mg/month) over a 2–3year period. Multiple formulations are avail able and require intramuscular injection, gel, or patch application [118].
paragraphs.heading: and Fertility

paragraphs.text: Outside the subsequent risk of iatrogenic adrenal insufficiency from glucocorticoid treatment, ACTH deficiency (central adrenal insufficiency) in CCS is relatively uncommon. The pituitary-adrenal axis appears to be rela tively radio-resistant in patients irradiated for nonpituitary disorders, and clinically appar ent ACTH deficiency is uncommon (around 3%) in patients receiving a total radiation dose to the HP axis of <50 Gy, and virtually unre ported after TBI [28]. Cranial irradiation >18 Gy, patients with a history of craniopha ryngioma or medulloblastoma, or irradiated after age 16 years have an increased incidence of ACTH deficiency [124]. ACTH deficiency can result following pituitary surgery or from direct tumor extension into the pituitary. Primary adrenal insufficiency is usually the result of direct tumor extension into the adre nal gland or secondary to the use of an adrenal-toxic drug such as ketoconazole or mitotane [124].
paragraphs.heading: 38.4.4 Adrenal Axis

paragraphs.text: A study evaluating the hypothalamicpituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis of survivors of
paragraphs.heading: 38.4.4 Adrenal Axis

paragraphs.text: childhood ALL provided some evidence of HPA axis dysregulation: subjects had higher morning cortisol levels and increased cortisol suppression in response to oral dexametha sone compared to healthy age- and sexmatched controls [48, 125]. Higher cortisol levels in CCS were associated with fatigue and poorer quality of life. HPA axis dysregulation was thought to be secondary to chronic ste roids as part of ALL treatment or secondary to the stress of illness [125]. Annual screening for central adrenal insufficiency is necessary in CCS at risk with a morning sample of cor tisol; values <3 μg/dL are suggestive of insuf ficiency and values >15 μg/dL exclude insufficiency. If doubtful, dynamic tests should be performed [8, 93, 100]. Replace ment with hydrocortisone at maintenance doses and with stress dosing during illness are required [8, 34].

With the advances in the treatment of pediat ric cancers and the increase in the number of children surviving malignancy, it is necessary to know the consequences of different treat ment modalities, some of which may occur many years or even decades after cancer treatment. Endocrine abnormalities are fre quent consequences of cancer treatments. Lifelong follow-up of CCSs, including screen ing for endocrine dysfunction, is recom mended to ensure early diagnosis and appropriate treatment.

Misra (eds.), Pediatric Endocrinology, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-66296-6_38 ## PDF page 1004 | printed page 1008 Key Points 5 Advances in the treatment of pediatric cancers have resulted in increasing numbers of children surviving malig nancy. As a consequence of different modalities and intensity of treatment, the number of childhood cancer survi vors with acute and late consequences of malignancies and their treatment is also increasing. 5 Endocrine abnormalities are frequent consequences of cancer treatment, both acute and late onset, and vary widely by cancer type, treatment modalities, and patient characteristics. Lifelong followup of childhood cancer survivors, includ ing screening for endocrine dysfunction, is recommended to ensure early diagno sis and appropriate treatment. ### 38.1 Introduction Childhood cancer is the second leading cause of death in children aged 1–14 years, exceeded in the United States only by accidents [1]. About 400,000 children aged 0–19 years are estimated to develop cancer every year, approximately 90% in low- and middle-income countries [2]. Advances in the treatment of pediatric cancers have resulted in increasing numbers of children surviving their malig nancy, with current survival rates greater than 85% in 5 years in high-income countries [1]. ### 38 The most common childhood malignan cies are leukemias (28.8%), followed by cen tral nervous system (CNS) tumors (24.0%) and lymphomas (11.2%) [3]. Acute lympho blastic leukemia (ALL) accounts for about 80% of childhood leukemia cases [4]. Brain tumors are the largest group of solid tumors in children and adolescents, with medullo blastoma being the most frequent malignant neoplasm of the CNS [5]. Craniopharyngioma corresponds to 5–10% of pediatric CNS tumors [5]. Therapeutic options consist of multiagent chemotherapy, surgery, radiotherapy, and bone marrow or stem cell transplantation. As expected, decreased mortality from malig nancy comes at the cost of increased morbid ity resulting from acute and late effects of different treatment modalities. Endocrine dis orders affect up to 60% of childhood cancer survivors (CCS) and may occur soon after treatment or many years after cure of malig nancy [6]. Obesity, malnutrition, metabolic syndrome, secondary malignancies, and growth disturbances are frequent conse quences of cancer treatment during childhood [6]. Up to 49% of children who have under gone cranial irradiation developed at least one hormone deficiency. Growth hormone defi ciency (GHD) is the most frequent, followed by either thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) or gonadotropin deficiency. Adrenocortico tropic hormone (ACTH) deficiency is the least common and permanent diabetes insipidus (DI) is very rare [6–9]. Risk factors for endo crine deficiencies include total radiation dose, age at treatment, and time since last treatment [7]. More recently, immune checkpoint inhibi tors, such as ipilimumab, have been found to be associated with hypophysitis with or with out hypopituitarism, thyroid dysfunction, and, in rare cases, adrenalitis [10]. Therefore, lifelong follow-up of CCS, including screen ing for endocrine dysfunction, is recom mended to ensure early diagnosis and appropriate treatment. This chapter will describe the more frequently acute and late endocrine effects of cancer treatment during childhood. ### 38.2 Acute Endocrine Effects ### of Brain Tumors Treatment Children with tumors that involve the hypothalamic-pituitary (HP) region, such as craniopharyngiomas or germinomas, may present hypothalamic-pituitary axis (HPA) dysfunction before tumor treatment or soon after the therapeutic procedure. Growth fail ure, obesity, delayed puberty, and central DI related to compression and/or invasion of the HP axis are frequently seen. Deficiencies in GH, gonadotropins, and ACTH are reported in 75%, 60%, and 30% of patients, respectively [11, 12]. Whenever possible, a complete endo ## PDF page 1005 | printed page 1009 crinologic evaluation should be performed before initiating treatment [12]. Most cases of central DI are secondary to destruction or degeneration of the neurons originating in the supraoptic and paraventric ular nuclei and may be a presenting symptom of Langerhans cell histiocytosis, germinoma and craniopharyngioma. A destruction of 80–90% of the hypothalamic vasopressin (AVP) or antidiuretic hormone (ADH) neu rons is required to produce DI. As a result, even large lesions in the sellar and suprasellar area generally are not associated with impaired water homeostasis until they are sur gically resected. Intraoperative damage of AVP neurons during HP surgery is one of the most common causes of central DI, corre sponding to 20% of all cases [13]. Sodium alterations are common after transsphenoidal surgery (TSS) of the pitu itary gland, but they are generally transitory with normal AVP secretion and diuresis at 7–14 postoperative days [13]. Triphasic response that consists of initial central DI (1–4 days) followed by syndrome of inappro priate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) (4–7 days) due to the release of AVP from degenerating neurons, and finally, per manent DI is often noted after prolonged neurosurgery [14, 15]. Symptoms of DI are consisting of high-volume output of dilute urine, hypovolemia, and hypernatremia. Local edema at the surgical site and interruption of normal AVP secretion are thought to be caus ative. The duration of this first phase is vari able, so intravenous AVP infusion might be needed. Coexisting hypothyroidism and adre nal insufficiency may mask the symptoms of DI due to reduced free water clearance [16, 17]. Transient SIADH usually occurs 4–7 days postoperative and is associated with postop erative morbidity. It develops from the uncon trolled release of AVP by degenerating pituitary nerve terminals containing neurose cretory granules [15]. This unregulated release of AVP results in inappropriately decreased urinary output with high urinary osmolality (>200 mOsm/kg), hypervolemia, and mod estly elevated urinary sodium concentrations (>20–30 mEq/L). Fluid restriction is recom mended for treatment [18–20]. Finally, if more than 90% of AVP neurons are damaged, patients develop the third phase of permanent DI. At this point, the treatment of choice for central DI is intranasal or oral desamino-darginine vasopressin (DDAVP). Another hyponatremic condition virtu ally indistinguishable from SIADH is cere bral salt wasting (CSW), a less common condition primarily seen, but not exclusively, in neurosurgical patients associated with CNS disease. In CSW, there is inappropriate and excessive release of natriuretic peptides leading to a primary natriuresis and volume depletion. The mechanism behind the devel opment of CSW probable involves disrup tion of neural input to the kidneys along with the stimulated release of natriuretic fac tors. The main difference is the absence or presence of volume depletion: CSW presents with hyponatremia, clinical evidence of dehydration (not always present), inappro priately concentrated urine, and renal sodium wasting, often in the setting of acute head injury, bleed, or surgery. It may be differenti ated from SIADH based on the persistence of hypouricemia and increased fractional excretion of urate following the correction of hyponatremia. The preferred therapy for the treatment of hyponatremia in patients with CSW is 3% sodium chloride [19, 20]. ### 38.3 Malnutrition, Cachexia, ### Weight Gain, and Hyperglycemia During Cancer Treatment During treatment for pediatric cancer, mal nutrition, and cachexia are common situa tions. Chemotherapy, radiation, surgery, and immunotherapy directly result in nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, malabsorption, stomati tis, esophagitis, and anorexia. Malnutrition can compromise immunity leading to higher infection rates, neuropathy, worse physical function and quality of life [21]. Tumorinduced cytokine production initiates a cas cade of metabolic events including glycogenolysis, lipolysis, proteolysis, increased resting energy expenditure, and ## PDF page 1006 | printed page 1010 gluconeogenesis [22]. It should be noted that pediatric patients with ALL can experience significant weight gain at the beginning of treatment secondary to reduced physical activity and to high-dose glucocorticoid treatment [23]. Hyperglycemia, insulin resis tance, dyslipidemia, central adiposity, and hepatic steatosis may also be precipitated by glucocorticoids [24]. l-asparaginase, which is often combined with glucocorticoids in the treatment of ALL, has toxic effects on the beta-cell and has been associated with the development of transient or persistent diabe tes mellitus [25]. ### 38.4 Late Endocrine Effects ### of Cancer Treatment During Childhood 6 26 6 9 26 ### 38 27 28 29 30 6 9 38.1 Table 38.1 Common hypothalamic-pituitary late effects in survivors of childhood cancer Radiotherapy (type and dose) Hypothalamicpituitary disorderb Total body irradiation (≥10 Gy single dose or ≥12 Gy fractionated) GH deficiency Cranial radiotherapy (18–30 Gy) GH deficiency Central precocious puberty Cranial radiotherapy (≥30 Gy) GH deficiency Central precocious puberty LH/FSH deficiencya TSH deficiencya ACTH deficiencya Sklar et al. GHD may appear after 12 months if the dose is greater than 60 Gy, in 36 months if the dose is between 25 and 30 Gy, and in 60 months if the dose is between 15 to 20 Gy [41]. Antipituitary and antihypothalamus autoanti bodies were demonstrated in 47.8% of children irradiated due to craniopharyngioma, germi noma, or gliomas, compared with none in 50 healthy controls [43]. This implies that RT may have an indirect effect by triggering an inappro priate immune attack on the pituitary tissues by autoantibodies [7]. Spinal irradiation is an inde pendent risk factor for growth impairment and may result in disproportionate growth more evi dent during puberty [44]. GHD is unlikely after traditional chemo therapy, but some newer agents may interfere with normal growth by affecting growth plates or dysregulating growth hormone-insulin-like growth factor-I (GH-IGF-I) signaling path ways (tyrosine kinase inhibitors, TKI) or caus ing an autoimmune hypophysitis (immune checkpoint inhibitors) [34, 45]. Some alkylat ing agents, such as busulfan and lomustine, are independent risk factor for short stature, par ticularly after leukemia or neuroblastoma, and are also risk factors for gonadal dysfunction, which may further exacerbate growth impair ment [30]. Other chemotherapy agents may directly damage the growth plates and cause severe short stature, such as cis-retinoic acid for the treatment of neuroblastoma and hedge hog pathway inhibitors [46, 47]. ### 38.4.1.1 Diagnosis of GHD After ### Cancer Treatment Growth of children who have undergone can cer treatment should be assessed every 6–12 months, and lifelong assessment may be necessary to screen for the development of GHD. It is recommended to measure standing and sitting height in children treated with spi nal radiotherapy, craniospinal irradiation, as well as radiation to the chest, abdomen, or pelvis [26, 48]. Establishing the diagnosis of GHD can be challenging and should be made in the context of clinical findings, as a growth deceleration of at least 0.3 SDS/year or height deviation from the familial background [49], and laboratory evaluation. It is important to avoid false-positive tests in the diagnosis of GHD, with special attention to obesity, a common condition in some CCS [50]. The Pediatric Endocrine Society guidelines suggest that the diagnosis of GHD without using a GH dynamic test can be made in patients with the following conditions: auxological criteria as mentioned before, HP defect (such as major congenital malformation, tumor, or irradia tion), and deficiency of at least one additional pituitary hormone [51]. In patients with a high probability of GHD (poor growth, other pitu itary hormones deficiencies), one GH provoc ative test is sufficient to make the diagnosis, after excluding other growth failure etiologies (e.g., total body irradiation, imatinib mesyl ate, and cis-retinoic acid treatment) [50]. The insulin tolerance test has been considered the gold standard provocative stimulation test to make the diagnosis of GHD, but caution should be exerted and alternative secreta gogues (i.e., glucagon) should be considered in patients at risk for seizures [50, 52, 53]. Growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) alone or in combination with arginine is not recom mended in CCS after HP irradiation because radiation doses less than 40 Gy cause predom inantly hypothalamic damage, and conse quently, exogenous hypothalamic hormones administration may cause false-negative results [26, 28]. Radiation-induced reduction of somatostatin secretion result in greater tonic GH release from the remaining somato trophs [37], and the decreased GH pulse amplitude has been shown to be secondary to decreased GHRH secretion [37]. GH neurose cretory dysfunction has been associated with low-dose radiation exposure, with a preserved peak GH response on dynamic tests, despite decreased endogenous GH secretion [54]. During puberty, these patients do not present ## PDF page 1008 | printed page 1012 an appropriate acceleration in growth velocity due to a lack of increased GH secretion [54, 55]. The measurement of serum IGF-I levels is not recommended as a biomarker for the diag nosis of GHD in CCS, especially among those exposed to HP irradiation [26]. Normal serum IGF-I and insulin-like growth factor binding protein-3 (IGFBP-3) levels have been observed in CCS who failed in GH dynamic testing, with abnormal growth velocity and GHD, especially those treated with low doses of radiotherapy [56, 57]. The use of IGF-I as a screening tool should be restricted to patients treated with high cranial radiation doses [58]. ### 38.4.1.2 Treatment of GHD After ### Cancer Treatment Treatment with GH is usually indicated in CCS with proven GHD after careful discus sion with the patient, his/her family if appro priate, as well as with the treating oncologist or neurosurgeon. The most appropriate and safest time to start GH is still a topic of debate, primarily due to a paucity of data and lack of controlled trials [59]. The timing of initiation of GH therapy following comple tion of cancer therapy or treatment of an intracranial tumor depends on many factors and should be individualized, with reports of treatment starting as early as 3 months in chil dren with radiologically proven stable cranio pharyngiomas who have significant growth and metabolic disturbances [52]. The Endocrine Society and the Pediatric Endocrine Society guidelines suggest waiting for 12 months after completing cancer treatments [26, 51]. In children with residual tumor and stable disease, as is often the case with optic pathway tumors and low-grade gliomas, the safety and timing of the initiation of GH treatment should specifically be discussed with the oncologist [26]. GH doses are similar to those used for the treatment of GHD in non-CCS [26, 51], with a starting dose of 0.022–0.035 mg/kg/day and individualization of subsequent dosing [51]. Long-acting GH preparations have different pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics than daily GH [60, 61], and current safety data in CCS are very limited [52]. The safety of GH replacement for children on treatment with TKI has not ### 38 been established and therefore is not recom mended at the present time [26, 52]. 52 26 49 51 52 53 62 38.2 GH replacement therapy has been shown to increase growth velocity and adult height in CCS with GHD [29, 63]. Primary hypothyroidism is reported in 4%, 7%, and 13% after a mean thyroid irradiation dose of 10, 20, and 30 Gy, respectively [82]. Subclinical hypothyroidism is more common and may be transient. The younger the age, the higher the risk, with the greatest risk before 5 years of age. While most patients (65%) will develop primary hypothy roidism 5 years or more after radiation [83, 84], the risk of developing radiation-related hypothyroidism remains elevated even >25 years after exposure [84]. Benign nodules and thyroid malignancies can also occur after head and neck irradiation or TBI before BMT [85–88]. Given the impact of thyroid status on growth and development, appropriate lifelong monitoring is necessary to recognize these dis ### 38 orders and initiate appropriate treatment [87]. Annual thyroid and cervical lymph node eval uation on physical examination and annual free thyroxine and TSH measurements are necessary after external radiation or 131I-metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG), and before and periodically during immunother apy or TKI therapy (sunitinib). In thyrotoxic patients, thyrotropin receptor antibody (TRAb) should be measured to assess for autoimmune thyroid disease. Ultrasonogra phy and fine needle aspiration biopsy are indi cated if a palpable abnormality is identified [87]. However, small or posterior nodules may not be appreciated by palpation. Although there are no formal guidelines regarding the use of thyroid ultrasonography for regular screening for secondary thyroid malignancies, it is suggested to start the assessment 5 years after radiotherapy or MIBG treatment and it might be repeated every 3–5 years [48, 89, 90]. Children treated for Hodgkin disease have a relative risk for hypothyroidism of 17.1 times compared with sibling controls; in patients treated with 45 Gy or more, the risk of hypo thyroidism is 50% at 20 years from diagnosis [82]. Other agents known to cause primary hypothyroidism are MIBG, 131-iodine, TKI, immune checkpoint inhibitors, interferon-α, and interleukin-2 [45, 87]. After the last drug exposure, hypothyroidism may be preceded by a thyrotoxic phase due to destructive thyroid itis [87]. To mitigate the risks to the thyroid gland during MIBG therapy, potassium iodide alone or in combination with potassium per chlorate or methimazole and exogenous thy roxine have been used to block thyroidal uptake, with conflicting results [87]. Children with CNS tumors near the hypothalamus or optic pathways are at increased risk of CPP [8]. CPP or puberty acceleration can also occur after cranial radio therapy (18–50 Gy) to any area of the CNS, not necessarily the HP region, and CPP is consid ered by some authors to be the second most common endocrine dysfunction after radio therapy [95]. Risk factors are young age, female sex, and increased BMI. Girls are more affected than boys following lower-dose irradiation (16–24 Gy), while higher radiation doses (25–50 Gy) lead to CPP in both sexes equally [96, 97]. The mechanism for CPP following irra diation is hypothesized to involve the dysregula tion of cortical influences on the hypothalamus and the release of the inhibitory GABAnergic tone [96, 98, 99]. Testicular volume may be a less reliable indicator of pubertal onset in boys who have received gonadotoxic chemotherapy and/or testicular radiation. Damage to the sem iniferous tubules during treatment may result in atrophic testes that are incapable of enlarging during pubertal progression. Therefore, the assessment of other secondary sexual charac teristics on physical examination is necessary [100]. The increase in growth velocity due to puberty can delay the diagnosis of GHD, or a blunted or absent growth spurt due to concom itant GHD may occur. Treatment with a depot gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) analogue may be indicated [95]. ### 38.4.3.2 Delayed Puberty, ### Hypogonadism, and Fertility Delayed puberty and hypogonadism are fre quent complications in CCS. Delayed puberty can result from primary gonadal injury (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism) or defi ciency of central activating signals (hypogo nadotropic hypogonadism) [34, 101]. CCS patients at risk of hypogonadism must be asked about onset and tempo of puberty, and menstrual history, and Tanner staging should be performed annually until sexual maturity [34]. High-dose cranial irradiation (>40 Gy) affects the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal ## PDF page 1012 | printed page 1016 (HPG) axis and is associated with hypogo nadotropic hypogonadism within the context of combined hormonal pituitary deficiencies [7, 101]. CCS with a history of exposure to radiotherapy, including abdominal/pelvic, TBI, and craniospinal radiation, and/or alkyl ating agents are at increased risk of gonadal failure. Additionally, gonadal failure had been described in patients after treatment with 131-radioiodine for differentiated thyroid car cinoma, and after MIBG for neuroblastoma treatment [34]. The main chemotherapeutic agents with a gonadotoxic effect are the alkylating agents, alone or in combination. It is difficult to establish the isolated effect of each medica tion, as protocols generally use them in com bination, so the dose equivalent to cyclophosphamide (CED) must be calculated. The use of CED >6000 mg/m2 is a high-risk factor for gonadal failure. TKIs, in addition to causing central hypogonadism due to hypophysitis, can induce an inflammatory response in the gonads, leading to gonadal dysfunction and infertility [34, 101–103]. Radiotherapy worsens the gonadotoxic effect of alkylating agents [34, 101]. BMT can affect the gonads during conditioning, with the use of gonadotoxic drugs, associated with or without whole-body radiation and high-dose glucocorticoids. About 83% of patients will have hypogonadism after BMT [8, 9, 88]. Diagnosis of hypogonadism is based on laboratory testing, which includes morning LH, FSH, and total testosterone (boys) or estradiol (girls) levels, and bone age radiogra phy to assess skeletal maturity until epiphy seal fusion [8, 48, 88, 103]. As primary and central hypogonadism can coexist in CCS with multiple therapies, LH and FSH will have little diagnostic value in these patients [8]. Treatment should be initiated at adequate age for both sexes [48, 88, 103]. Surgical, med ical, and technological advances have enabled the medical community to provide fertility options for patients with cancer and cancer survivors. Discussion of the impact of cancer treatment on fertility and a review of options of fertility preservation are recommended during cancer diagnosis and treatment with patients and their families [104–113]. ### 38 ### 38.4.3.3 Female Hypogonadism ### and Fertility Hypogonadism may be suspected in CCS girls with no signs of puberty at 13 years-old, failure in pubertal progression, menstrual irregularity, primary amenorrhea at 16 years, or secondary amenorrhea [34, 48, 88]. Chemotherapy drugs, particularly alkylating drugs such as busulfan, cyclophosphamide, lomustine, and procarba zine, are harmful to the ovaries by causing damage to the DNA of the growing follicles and germ cells depletion. Older age and more advanced pubertal stage are susceptible to lower doses with reduction of ovarian follicles and premature ovarian insufficiency (POI). POI is a clinical condition characterized by the absence of menstrual cycles for 4 or more months and two elevated serum FSH levels in the menopausal range at an age younger than 40 years [103]. Ovarian damage occurs due to direct exposition to radiation during pelvic or low abdominal, lumbosacral, spinal, and TBI, and depends on the dose, number of fractions, and age of exposure to radiotherapy. Ovaries of younger girls are more resistant to damage from irradiation [114, 115]. Increasing ovarian irradiation dose and exposure to procarbazine and cyclophosphamide at ages 13–20 years are independent risk factors for the development of acute ovarian failure [114] . Decreased ovarian reserve can be demon strated by low anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) levels, low ovarian surface area, and high FSH levels [103, 114]. AMH is produced by the granulosa cells of preantral and small antral follicles and is present at low levels in prepubertal females and increases to a peak around age 25 years. It decreases with age, and with the decreasing reserve of ovarian folli cles. It is not recommended as a screening for POI, but it might be used to assess female fer tility at greater than 25 years [88, 103, 114]. Radiation affects not only the ovary but also the uterus and can cause vascular injury, endothelial damage and fibrosis in the myo metrium, increasing the risk of miscarriage, preterm delivery, small for gestational age birth, and postpartum hemorrhage, with impact on younger women [114]. Some stud ies have shown that ovarian dysfunction can be transient and may not require hormone ## PDF page 1013 | printed page 1017 replacement [116]. Spontaneous recovery of gonadal function after TKI may occur [102]. Some patients will have permanent POI with infertility and estrogen deficiency, but others will show recovery allowing fertility, although their reproductive life may be shorter [88, 103]. Alkylating agents and radiation dose of >30 Gy or ovarian/uterine radiation doses ≥5 Gy are associated with a decreased proba bility of spontaneous pregnancy [117]. Treatment for female hypogonadism aims to induce and maintain secondary sexual char acteristics, to promote growth without acceler ating fusion of the growth plates, normalize uterine growth, avoid sexual dysfunction, and promote proper acquisition of bone mass. Induction of thelarche is achieved by using estrogen with gradual dose escalation starting at 11–12 years of age until menarche is achieved. After menarche (or after 2 years of starting estrogen replacement if no spontane ous bleeding occurs), progesterone must be added to promote cycling, in the same scheme as for other causes of hypogonadism. However, 17-β-estradiol is the treatment of choice [118]. However, for convenience, a combination estrogen-progestin oral contraceptive pill can be introduced after the patient is on full replace ment doses of estrogen. Delaying the onset of puberty in girls who were diagnosed late and have short stature should be discussed with the girl and her family. Hypopituitary women treated with GH should receive estrogen replacement preferably by a nonoral route, as oral estrogen reduces serum IGF-I response to GH therapy [119]. To reduce the cytotoxic effects of radiation and chemotherapy, some investigators have tried maintaining germinal epithelium quiescence by creating an artificial prepubescent state using a GnRH agonist [106, 108, 120]. However, there are no current con sensus guidelines on the use of GnRH agonists to preserve fertility during chemotherapy and/ or radiotherapy [34, 106]. ### 38.4.3.4 Male Hypogonadism ### and Fertility Hypoandrogenism may manifest clinically as delayed or arrested puberty: no signs of puberty after 14 years of age, or absence of pubertal progress over 6–8 months. Annual assessment of pubertal development is recom mended until sexual maturity for CCS treated with gonadotoxic therapy before the onset of puberty. Testicular volume may not increase as expected during puberty in patients who received gonadotoxic therapy [34, 48, 121, 122]. Young men treated with gonadotoxic therapies after puberty should be assessed annually for symptoms of hypoandrogenism (decreased libido, decreased spontaneous erections, gynecomastia, loss of body hair, decreased muscle bulk or testicular volume, and hot flashes) [123]. A possible association between gynecomastia and TKI use has been reported [45]. Testicular radiation, gonadotoxic chemo therapy, orchiectomy, cranial surgery, or cen tral radiation involving the HP axis can result in primary or secondary hypogonadism. Testicular tissue is more sensitive to radiation than ovarian tissue, and Sertoli cells are com paratively more sensitive than Leydig cells. In adults, testicular damage has been described at doses between 0.2–0.7 Gy, with an increase in FSH levels and changes in semen analysis. Exposure to conditioning doses of 10–12 Gy during TBI before puberty may lead to small testicular volume in the adult with damage of the seminiferous tubules and spermatogonia [121, 123]. Low doses of radiation, such as the 2 Gy used in TBI, and low doses of chemo therapy can deplete the spermatogonia pool through direct DNA damage resulting in per manent infertility [121, 123]. Azoospermia is described with doses of 6–10 Gy and Leydig cell failure with doses ≥20 Gy. In the series of CCS treated with chemotherapy and radio therapy at doses of 30–45 Gy, it was reported that 83% suffered from azoospermia. However, 17% recovered spermatogenesis 12–15 years after treatment [101, 121–123]. Inhibin B secreted by Sertoli cells can be use ful for screening for gonadal damage. In pre pubescent children, together with FSH, it can be used to assess gonadotoxic potential [101, 103, 122]. Testosterone replacement is the primary treatment for male hypogonadism. The goals of therapy are similar to girls to induce normal pubertal development, maintain secondary sexual characters, avoid sexual dysfunction, ## PDF page 1014 | printed page 1018 improve bone density, and increase lean mass. Testosterone replacement may be initiated at 14 years of age at low doses (50 mg/month) and increased every 6 months to reach full adult replacement (200–250 mg/month) over a 2–3year period. Multiple formulations are avail able and require intramuscular injection, gel, or patch application [118]. ### 38.4.4 Adrenal Axis Outside the subsequent risk of iatrogenic adrenal insufficiency from glucocorticoid treatment, ACTH deficiency (central adrenal insufficiency) in CCS is relatively uncommon.
